opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting shifts happening right now. Traditionally, drug design has been a very slow, iterative process. A medicinal chemist comes up with an idea for a molecule, it gets synthesized, tested in the lab, and you learn something, but each loop can take weeks or months. You're only ever exploring a tiny sliver of chemical space, which is astronomically large; there are something like ten to the sixty possible drug-like molecules.

What generative models give us is the ability to explore that space far more broadly and far more intelligently. Instead of hand-designing each candidate, you can have models that propose molecules conditioned on what you care about: binding to the target, selectivity, the right properties for something that could actually become a medicine. And critically, you can pair that with predictive models, things like structure prediction and binding affinity models, that let you evaluate those ideas in silico before you ever touch a pipette.

The agentic piece is where it gets really interesting for me. Coming from a background in reinforcement learning and agents, I think of drug design as a search and decision-making problem. You have a goal, a huge space of actions, and expensive, noisy feedback. An agent can take generative proposals, score them with a whole stack of models, reason about trade-offs, decide which experiments are actually worth running, and then learn from the results. So rather than replacing the chemist, you're giving them a system that can run thousands of these design cycles computationally and come back with a much richer set of options.

The long-term vision is that more and more of that design loop happens in the computer, and the lab becomes the place where you validate and refine rather than where you do all the exploration. That's how you go from drug discovery being a bit of a lottery to something much more like engineering.

r001.rationale: It says predictive models can evaluate proposed molecules in silico, allowing broader exploration without searching the entire molecular space.

r002.rationale: It describes chemical space as enormous and traditional exploration as limited, but does not infer that many viable designs may exist for a given therapeutic target.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to frame it is: the space of possible drug-like molecules is enormous. People throw around numbers like ten to the sixty, and whatever the exact figure is, it's far beyond anything you could ever enumerate or screen, even computationally. So the traditional way of exploring that space has been quite local. You start from a hit, a chemist makes some modifications, you test, you iterate. It works, but it's slow, and you end up only ever looking in a tiny neighbourhood of what's actually possible.

Generative models change that in a pretty fundamental way, because rather than searching the space, you're learning a model of it. You can condition on the properties you care about, binding to a particular target, selectivity against related targets, solubility, toxicity, and have the model propose molecules that satisfy those constraints directly. So you're not stepping through chemical space one edit at a time, you're sampling from the regions that look promising. And importantly those models get better the more data you feed back into them.

That's where the agent piece comes in for me. Having a good generative model on its own isn't enough, because drug discovery is this long multistep process with lots of decisions. Which hypothesis to pursue, which molecules to actually synthesise, which assays to run, how to interpret the results and update your beliefs. An agent can sit on top of the generative models, the predictive models, and the physical simulations, and actually drive that loop. It proposes, it tests, in silico or in the lab, it observes, and it chooses the next experiment. That closed loop is really the thing that lets you explore far more of the space than any human team could, and more systematically.

What I find exciting is that this brings in a lot of the ideas from reinforcement learning and search that we saw work in games. You have a model of the world, you have an objective, and you have an agent that learns to plan over long horizons under uncertainty. Chemistry and biology are obviously much harder environments than a board game, the simulators are imperfect and experiments are expensive and noisy. But the structure of the problem is quite similar, and I think we're at the point where the models are good enough to start doing that in earnest.

r001.rationale: The response describes predictive models working with generative models to guide proposals toward promising regions, avoiding step-by-step exploration of the enormous molecular space.

r002.rationale: It notes the molecular space is enormous and traditional exploration is local, but does not state that successful drug discovery without AI indicates many viable designs for a given therapeutic target.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting shift is from searching through the molecules you already have to designing the molecules you actually want. The space of possible molecules is enormous, so you’re never going to explore it exhaustively. You need models that can guide you toward promising regions of that space.

With generative models, you can propose a molecule conditioned on the properties you’re looking for. And it’s not just, does it bind to a particular target? You also care about selectivity, toxicity, whether you can make it, and how it behaves in the body. Those objectives can pull in different directions, which makes this a really interesting design problem.

Agents could help connect that design process to a broader experimental loop: propose a hypothesis, choose what to test, look at the results, and use those results to decide what to do next. The crucial thing is that the loop stays grounded in experiments. Generating a plausible molecule isn’t the same as discovering a drug. For me, the opportunity is to make each experiment more informative, so that we learn faster and explore possibilities we might otherwise have missed.

r001.rationale: It says the molecular space is too large to explore exhaustively and that models can guide exploration toward promising regions.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss drug discovery without AI or infer that many viable designs may exist for a given therapeutic target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting shift is from searching through molecules we already know how to make to generating molecules that could have the properties we actually want. The space of possible molecules is enormous, so the challenge is deciding which tiny fraction of that space is worth exploring.

Generative models give us a way to propose candidates, but proposing a molecule is only one part of the problem. Does it bind to the target? Is it selective? Can you make it? Will it get to the right place in the body? Those objectives have to come together.

That’s where agents become interesting: connecting molecule generation to predictive models, simulations, and experimental results, then using that feedback to decide what to try next. You get an iterative process of designing, testing, and learning. The ambition is to make each experiment more informative and increase the chance that the molecules we pursue become useful medicines.

r001.rationale: The response says the molecular space is enormous and describes connecting generation to predictive models and feedback to decide what to try next, guiding exploration of a small fraction rather than searching it all.

r002.rationale: It mentions the enormous molecular space and desired properties, but does not say that successful drug discovery without AI shows many viable designs may exist for a given target.
